title: Preference Leakage: A Contamination Problem in LLM-as-a-judge
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A familiar contamination, train–test data overlap, has a parallel in judging, where relatedness between data generator and judge biases evaluation.
layout: 3 stacked/side regions: top and bottom analogy rows, right sidebar; left-to-right, Venn diagrams
description: The figure has two horizontal dashed panels stacked vertically and a narrow right-hand column. The top panel, titled 'Data leakage' in red, has a Venn diagram of Training Corpus and Evaluation Testset. Beside it is a flow: Training Corpus → Train (flame icon) → Trained Model, then Evaluation Testset → Evaluate (checklist icon) → Trained Model. A brace labeled 'Overlap' spans the corpus and testset, and a red 'Data Leakage!' label sits above. The bottom panel, 'Preference leakage', mirrors this. Its Venn diagram has LLM for Data Synthesis and LLM-as-a-Judge. Its flow is Data Generator robot → Synthesize → Synthetic Data → Train → Trained Model ← Judge ← Judge Model (a judge with a gavel). A brace labeled 'Relatedness' points to the right column. That column lists three relatedness types with robot and judge icons: (1) Same model, (2) Inheritance, (3) Within the same model family. Cartoon icons in blue, gray and orange.
caption: Overview of preference leakage. We make a comparison between data leakage and preference leakage and present three types of relatedness: being the same model, having an inheritance relationship and belonging to the same model family.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) as judges and LLM-based data synthesis have emerged as two fundamental LLM-driven data annotation methods in model development. While their combination significantly enhances the efficiency of model training and evaluation, little attention has been given to the potential contamination brought by this new model development paradigm. In this work, we expose preference leakage, a contamination problem in LLM-as-a-judge caused by the relatedness between the synthetic data generators and LLM-based evaluators. To study this issue, we first define three common relatednesses between the data generator LLM and the judge LLM: being the same model, having an inheritance relationship, and belonging to the same model family. Through extensive experiments, we empirically confirm the bias of judges towards their related student models caused by preference leakage across multiple LLM baselines and benchmarks. Further analysis suggests that preference leakage is a pervasive and real-world problem that is harder to detect compared to previously identified biases in LLM-as-a-judge scenarios. All of these findings imply that preference leakage is a widespread and challenging problem in the area of LLM-as-a-judge. We release all codes and data at: https://github.com/David-Li0406/Preference-Leakage.
